title: Care of Children in Early Years
summary: The first three years are the foundation years. Children form relationships through the consistent, continuous presence of caregivers who talk, feed, play and give love. Principle 1 — supportive and responsive environment: regular response to feeding, bodily needs and tactile comfort, the primary needs of children, gives a secure base and helps them regulate emotions. Principle 2 — responsive relationships and strong life skills: eye contact, pleasant gestures and hugs whenever the baby babbles or cries form new neural connections; routines, creative play and modelled social behaviour build independence and coping. Principle 3 — reduce sources of stress: respond on demand with multi-sensory interaction; protect children from loud noise, disturbing visuals and harsh movements; do not leave them alone or ignore them.

Breast milk is best: a complete food for the first six months (no supplements needed), it protects from infection, builds immunity, reduces illness and death, and gives touch and comfort. Weaning starts after six months — the move from breast milk to semi-solid foods such as dalia, sooji kheer, khichdi and ragi; many cultures mark it with a ceremony. Lactating mothers need cereals, pulses, fruits, vegetables, nuts, dairy (and meat, fish, eggs if non-vegetarian) and plenty of fluids.

Clothing for newborns should be soft, loose and clean, never left wet. Babies sleep about 18 hours a day; total sleep falls with age but night sleep lengthens. Exercise grows from moving limbs to rolling, creeping, crawling and pulling up; games with infants are good exercise.

Immunisation makes a person resistant to an infectious disease, usually by a vaccine; an immunisation card is made soon after birth. Schedule: birth — BCG, OPV, Hepatitis B; 6, 10 and 14 weeks — DPT, OPV, Hepatitis B, HiB, pneumococcal (IPV at 10 and 14 weeks); 6 months — rotavirus, influenza; 9 months — measles; 12 months — varicella; 15 months — MMR, pneumococcal booster; 18 months — OPV, DPT, HiB booster, Hepatitis A; 2 years — typhoid; 4 years — MMR; 5 years — OPV, DPT booster. Cleanliness and hygiene (wiping eyes, nose, nails) protect from infection.

Stimulation builds neural pathways in the brain and motor and problem-solving skills through sight, sound, smell, taste and touch; activities should be many and repeated. Visual: faces, colours and shapes; keeping the face close, facial gestures, eye contact, peek-a-boo. Auditory: talking in a soft, babyish voice, music and rhythm, natural sounds of birds and animals build the base for language. Touch: gentle holding and rocking give trust; rough handling causes stress; soft toys and new textures (food, sponges, cloth). Kinaesthetic (sense of movement): lifting, rocking and swaying to rhythm, crawling over and under objects, clapping and snapping.
## Early years as the foundation for later learning

Quality childcare decides how children learn and relate. Conditions for a safe, nurturing, stimulating setting: low child-caregiver ratio, small group size, motivated and sensitive caregivers, positive caregiver-child interaction, age-appropriate activities and materials, good health, hygiene and safety, and trained staff. Interest is a form of energy that leads to curiosity and motivation; adults' enthusiastic response keeps it alive. Positive relationships build independence, self-esteem and social skills; cognitive stimulation depends on early attachment and positive relationships. Sensory play supports brain, language, motor, cognitive and social development. Routines and rhythms of caregiving give security, predictability and control over the environment.
## Care settings and the parent–teacher partnership

Care may be familial (home, by parents or relatives) or non-familial (babysitters, neighbours, crèches, day-care centres, preschools, nursery schools, workplace crèches); it may be home-based or centre-based. Parents, teachers and children form a dynamic triad. Children need unconditional love, safe surroundings, supportive teachers, play with other children, self-confidence and guidance. Parents and teachers should meet in workshops, talk daily at drop-off and pick-up, and use phone or messages to track milestones and spot delays early; sensitive responses relieve children's stress, as in the example of an 18-month-old who caught up within four months under a caring caregiver.

(i) A safe and nurturing environment that promotes physical, social, emotional and intellectual development. (ii) Familial (home-based) and non-familial (centre-based) care.

objective: Answer briefly: (i) What are the benefits of breastfeeding for babies? (ii) Why is it important for caregivers to ensure comfortable clothing for children?

(i) Breast milk is a complete food that protects from infection, builds immunity, reduces illness and death, and gives comfort. (ii) A baby's skin is soft and delicate; soft, loose, clean clothes protect it from stiff materials and discomfort.

case.passage: The first three years are often called the foundation years as incredible growth takes place in all domains of development. Children form relationships through the consistent and continuous presence of caregivers who talk, feed, play and give love and care. Regular response to feeding, bodily needs and tactile comfort are the primary needs of children. Caregivers promote healthy brain development by giving warmth, making eye contact and responding with a pleasant gesture or a hug every time the baby babbles or cries; this forms new neural connections in the brain. Reducing stress means responding to children on demand and protecting them from loud noise, disturbing visuals and harsh, fast movements. Leaving children alone or ignoring them can obstruct their growth and development.
items: Why are the first three years called the foundation years?
Because incredible growth takes place in all domains of development during these years.
Through the consistent and continuous presence of caregivers who talk, feed, play and give love and care.
Name the primary needs of children mentioned in the passage.
Regular response to feeding, bodily needs and tactile comfort.
How do warm responses help the baby's brain?
They form new neural connections in the brain.
Fill in the blank: Reducing stress means responding to children on ________.
Name two things from which caregivers should protect young children.
Any two: loud noise, disturbing visuals, harsh and fast movements, being left alone or ignored.

vsa: Mention any four conditions that generally foster a safe, nurturing and stimulating environment for children.

Any four: low child-caregiver ratio; small group size; motivated and sensitive caregivers; positive caregiver-child interaction; age- and developmentally appropriate activities and materials; good health, hygiene and safety practices; trained staff with professional development.
What care and protection should an ECCE worker take for children in the centre?

Keep the centre physically safe and supervise children all the time; ensure hygiene, clean water and safe food; follow immunisation and health check-ups; respond warmly to children's needs and protect them from stress, rough handling and neglect so they feel emotionally secure.
Why are routines important in caregiving?

Routines give children security and control over their environment and prepare them emotionally for coming changes. Familiar schedules and objects bring continuity and soothe them in times of change; babies learn time, sequence and permanence through the rhythms of care.
Why is interest important in a child's learning?

Interest is a form of energy that leads to curiosity and motivates and guides children's engagement with the world. Without interest there is no curiosity, no exploration and no real learning; enthusiastic adult response keeps it alive.

vsa: What is kinaesthetic stimulation? Give two activities.

Kinaesthetic means the sense of movement — exploring physical space by moving the body. Activities: lifting the baby up and down in different positions; rocking and swaying to a rhythm; letting the baby crawl over, under and through objects; clapping and snapping while talking.
sa: Explain the significance of sensory stimulation for development.

Infants learn about the world through their senses. Stimulation through sight, sound, smell, taste and touch creates neural pathways in the brain that support later learning, and develops motor skills and the ability to solve simple problems. Visual stimulation (faces, colours, peek-a-boo) builds observation; auditory input (talking, music, natural sounds) builds the base of language; touch (holding, rocking, textures) builds trust and fine motor skills; movement builds balance. Activities should be many and repeated.

sa: What role can teachers and parents play in relieving stress among children?

Young children cannot say what troubles them, so they show it by irritability or crying. Parents and teachers should respond sensitively to unusual behaviour, keep routines and familiar objects, give warm physical comfort, listen when children talk about school ('Teacher does not smile'), share information daily so home and centre feel like extensions of each other, and work as a team rather than against each other.
What are the different kinds of caregiving systems?

Familial care: by parents or relatives (aunts, uncles, grandparents) at home. Non-familial care: by non-relatives such as babysitters, neighbours or friends in the child's or the provider's home. Organised childcare: crèches, day-care centres, preschools, nursery schools, kindergartens and pre-primary schools, and workplace crèches. Care is also classed as home-based (few children in the provider's home) or centre-based (larger groups in a non-home setting).
Describe the principles of caregiving of children under three years.

Supportive and responsive environment: regular response to feeding, bodily needs and tactile comfort gives a secure base and helps children regulate emotions. Responsive relationships and strong life skills: warmth, eye contact, gestures and hugs build neural connections; routines and creative play build independence, curiosity and coping. Reduce sources of stress: respond on demand with multi-sensory interaction and protect children from loud noise, disturbing sights and harsh movements; never leave them alone or ignore them.
la: How can parents and teachers work together to support children's development?

Parents, teachers and children are a dynamic triad. Together they must create a nurturing, healthy and safe environment, pass on cultural values and help children master developmental tasks. Children need unconditional love, safe surroundings, supportive teachers, play with peers, self-confidence and guidance. Collaboration: centres keep regular contact; parent workshops share childcare practices and ways of discipline; daily exchanges at drop-off and pick-up track milestones and spot delays early. Channels: appointments for special issues, daily conversations, sharing home routines, email, messages and phone. Children's views: parents should listen when children talk about school; sensitive responses from both relieve stress. They must work as a team, not in opposition.

la: Why are the early years the foundation for later learning? Discuss the role of play and playful interactions in children's development.

Early childhood is a period of rapid development; quality care gives a safe, nurturing environment and decides how children learn and build relationships, while a poor start wastes human potential. Low ratios, small groups, sensitive trained caregivers and stimulating materials are needed. Play and playful interaction: from birth children explore through their senses; sensory play encourages discovery, independent thinking, imagination and creativity. It supports brain development (learning, memory), language (new words, songs), fine and gross motor skills (squeezing, pushing, throwing), cognitive growth (manipulating materials, new concepts), social interaction (sand and water play together) and body and space awareness.
